summary: Clarifies when a standards track RFC may refer normatively to a document at a lower maturity level, such as an informational RFC. It explains that exceptions to the usual rule are sometimes needed and describes how to handle them.

eli5.summary: Normally a serious rulebook should only rely on other equally serious rulebooks. This memo says when it may borrow from a less serious one.

questions: can a standards track rfc cite an informational rfc
what is a downward reference in an rfc
subtitle: When a standards track RFC may lean on a less mature document, and the Last Call step that makes it legitimate.

tldr.problem: IETF rules say a standards track RFC should not depend on a document at a lower maturity level, such as an Informational RFC. Sometimes there is no way around it, for example when an IETF document profiles an outside algorithm.
tldr.mechanism: The document says a downward reference is allowed if the need is stated explicitly in the normal IETF Last Call, so the community and the IESG can weigh in. Once a particular reference is accepted, an Area Director may waive repeating the notice.
tldr.outcome: It gives a clear route for justified exceptions without turning them into an easy way around the normal process. It is a Best Current Practice and has since been updated by RFC 4897 and RFC 8067.

today: RFC 3967 is a Best Current Practice that has been updated by RFC 4897 and RFC 8067, so read those alongside it. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Rule About Lower-Level References
sections.content:
The Internet Standards Process (RFC 2026, Section 4.2.4) says standards track specifications normally must not depend on other standards track specifications at a lower maturity level, or on non standards track specifications, other than specifications from other standards bodies. One intent is to avoid creating a perception that a standard is more mature than it actually is.

Best Current Practice documents have generally been treated like standards track documents here. A normative reference from a BCP to an Experimental RFC has been considered improper under RFC 2026.
sections.eli5: A very serious rulebook is supposed to lean only on other very serious rulebooks. Otherwise people might think it is more solid than it really is.

sections.title: What Counts as a Normative Reference
sections.content:
A normative reference names a document that must be read to fully understand or implement the new RFC, or whose contents are effectively part of it. An informative reference only gives background. The RFC admits that a precise definition has proven challenging in practice.

The test it offers: any document containing key information an implementer needs is normative. If you need a packet format or a required algorithm from another document, that reference is normative.

  • If a protocol relies on IPsec for security, the IPsec specification is needed to implement it, so the reference is normative.
  • In MIB documents, an IMPORTS clause is by definition a normative reference.
  • A reference to an example, such as text saying an algorithm like the one in some RFC would be acceptable, need not be normative.
sections.eli5: If you cannot finish the recipe without reading another page, that page is a must-read. If it is just a nice extra idea, it is only a suggestion.

sections.title: Why Downward References Are Needed
sections.content:
The RFC lists circumstances where a normative reference to a lower-level document conflicts with RFC 2026 but is still needed.

  • A standards track document may need to cite a protocol or algorithm from an external body that an IETF Informational RFC modified, adapted or profiled. The examples given are MD5 (RFC 1321) and HMAC (RFC 2104). This does not remove the IETF's duty to make sure the specification is clear enough for interoperable implementations.
  • A standards document may need to refer to a proprietary protocol, which the IETF normally documents in Informational RFCs.
  • A migration or co-existence document may need to define a standards track mechanism for moving from, or living alongside, a historic, proprietary or non-standards track protocol.
  • There may be exceptional procedural or legal reasons that force the target to be Informational or Historic, or at a lower level.
  • A BCP may want to describe best current practices for experimental or informational specifications.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the only place a needed idea is written down is in a lighter book. A rulebook about moving house from an old system has to talk about that old system, even if the old system is not a proper standard.

sections.title: The Last Call Procedure
sections.content:
For a Standards Track or BCP document that needs a normative reference to a lower-maturity document, the normal IETF Last Call is issued, and the need for the downward reference is explicitly documented in the Last Call itself. Community comments on whether the reference is appropriate are considered by the IESG as part of its deliberations.

Once a specific down reference to a particular document has been accepted by the community, for example because it has been mentioned in several Last Calls, an Area Director may waive the notice in later Last Calls. This should only happen when the same document and version are referenced, and when the AD believes its use is an accepted part of the community's understanding of the technical area. MD5 and HMAC are given as examples of well-known use among cryptographers.
sections.eli5: You have to announce it to everyone before you borrow from the lighter book. After the neighbors have seen the same borrowing a few times and are fine with it, a grown-up can skip the announcement.

sections.title: Limits and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The procedure is not an escape hatch. It should not be used if the proper step is to move the referenced document into the appropriate category. The RFC says it is not meant as an easy way out of normal process, but for specific cases where moving a particular document into the required category is problematic and unlikely ever to happen.

The Security Considerations section says the document is not known to create new vulnerabilities. It adds that inappropriate or excessive use of the process might be considered a downgrade attack on the quality of IETF standards or, worse, on the rigorous review of security aspects of standards.
sections.eli5: This is for real special cases, not for skipping homework. If you use it too much, the standards get sloppier, and that includes how carefully safety is checked.
